When I was little, I didn't twig that stardates weren't random numbers that an actor would invent on the spot. Though the math of stardates is known to be nonsensical, in the '90s-era shows stardates correspond to years in the Gregorian calendar:

1000 stardate units equaled one solar year

I was recently curious about when in the 24th century certain things are known to happen. I found afterward that I was stricken by a sense of loss. The universe suddenly seemed to have this exact endpointâ€” and it came and went 15 years ago with the finale of Voyager. That was my feeling. Wanting to know how true that actually was, I ventured further into Memory Alpha.

An executive summary

First, grounding: TNG was set mostly in the 2360s. Generations was in 2371, concurrent with Voyager and DS9. 2377 corresponds to stardates in the 54xxx range, and the last season of Voyager, which was two years after the end of DS9. TNG ended in 2370, with its series finale vision of the future set in 2395. As 2070 corresponds to 1994, that prospective future would correspond to 2019, in which year nature will render makeup and prosthetics unnecessary for making the cast look suitably aged. Maybe Captain Worf will happen by then?

But time does go on, as the "memory beta" division of the wiki shows. It's unsurprising to see a focus on Riker, whose story has much left unsaid at the end of TNG. Riker, if you don't know, captains his own ship from 2379 to 2385. He remained first officer of the Enterprise between the end of TNG and the end of Voyager.

The novel Imzadi presents Data as a commodore, commanding the Enterprise-F in the somewhat far-flung 2408.

But wait, didn't Data die? Of course he did: in 2379, during the events of Star Trek: Nemesis. My understanding from interviews is that Brent Spiner would be happy to get paid to play Data in voice, but can no longer reasonably represent an ageless manbot as his own meatbag shell continues to sag with the sands of time. Naturally, the "expanded universe" goes through some gymnastics to un-kill him:

In 2384, Data's memories were transferred into a new body designed and constructed by his father who at first transferred his own consciousness into the body in an effort to prolong his life for a continuation of his work on androids.

It only gets weirder, but at least books are still being written. There's a whole set of these, one as recently as January 2015.

Star Trek Online, released in 2010, begins some 50 years after TNG: 2409. It's fairly safe to assume that by that point Picard has given up command of the Enterprise, but you really can't put it past these people to have a 100+ year old dude still in uniform because they just won't let him die. I'm referencing one of the fan-made quasi-tv series here.

Part of STO's inner canon involved a recapitulation of everything post-Nemesis, and sounds fairly robust. The interesting thing about STO is that its developers have released periodic new content, the most recent batch on April 12th, 2016. They've even advanced the clock to 2410: The future of the future's future is here!

Tell me what shit to buy!

All of that said, I suppose it might seem like I've only kicked the can down the road: instead of 2377 (or 2379, I guess; I never watched Nemesis) it's 2411 where the Star Trek universe meets its heat-death, and events are limited to things we already know about from existing canon. But now I don't see it as being "over" in the same way. I mean, I see identity politics poisoning everything and think it's understood what jar jar abrams has been up to, but it's a big universe and hopefully people who aren't totally clueless haven't stopped dreaming about the future, in the context of Star Trek. Maybe, just maybe...

Now I turn the floor to you. How much of this stuff is worth reading? I'm all titillated with brain-pictures of TNG episodes that aren't reruns. I've read Imzadi and thought it was pretty decent. Maybe too big emotionally to be a TNG episode, but that's not a bad thing.

I, Q has a handful of discursions where John de Lancie dons his fedora and explains how stupid religion is. Having read many Victorian authors like H. Rider Haggard and Bram Stoker, I'm more accustomed to this sort of thing being both less restrained, and from the other end of the horseshoe, so to speak. Other than that, the book is a wacky romp. A bit meandering toward the end, but it's not too much longer than it needs to be.

I have a yellowed copy of The Wounded Sky (c. 1983) waiting next to my desk. An impulse thrift store buy. Probably an unabashed dime novel, but the description sounds like it has everything I like about ToS: hot aliens, ridiculous bullshit science, and dusky space-commies Klingons. Aw, yeeeeah.

Are the TNG books any good? Are they bogged down with progressivist autofellatio? Should I pay $20 + shipping for the first Titan novel?
